# Rapid Clicking on a 2004 Chrysler Concorde: Diagnosing Stalling and Start Issues

The symptom you are describingârapid clicking when turning the keyâis the classic acoustic signature of an ignition system that cannot draw sufficient current to engage the starter motor. On a 2004 Chrysler Concorde LXi with the 3.5L V6, this behavior often points to one of three specific failure modes: a weak battery, corroded or loose connections at the starter solenoid, or an internal fault within the starter assembly itself.

### The "Dead Battery" vs. Weak Alternator Cycle

Your initial report notes that the car started after sitting for 20 minutes. This is a textbook indicator of a battery that can no longer hold a charge under load but recovers slightly once restored to open-circuit voltage. When you shut off an engine, the alternator stops charging the battery immediately. If the battery is old or sulfated, its internal resistance rises. The starter motor on your 3.5L requires roughly 150 to 200 amps of instantaneous current to crank the engine. A marginal battery might show plenty of voltage with the headlights on (say, 12.4V) but drop to 9.6V or lower the moment the key is turned, causing the solenoid to click repeatedly without engaging the pinion gear.

You mentioned getting a new battery and charging the existing one, yet the clicking persisted. This suggests the alternator may not be maintaining proper voltage while the engine is running, or there is significant parasitic drain preventing the new battery from reaching full capacity before you attempt to start. Before assuming the starter is dead, verify that the system can sustain a load. Connect a digital multimeter across the battery terminals (positive and negative) with the engine running. If the reading does not stay above 13.5Vâ14.5V, the alternator is failing to recharge the battery, leading to the exact scenario you experienced: the car runs until the battery drains below the threshold required for starting.

### The Starter Solenoid and Connection Integrity

Once you have ruled out a charging system issue, the focus shifts to the physical connection between the battery and the starter solenoid. Even if the battery is new, corrosion or looseness at the cable terminals creates a high-resistance path. High resistance limits current flow, mimicking a dead battery by causing rapid clicking.

The most critical step here is to inspect the ground strap and the main positive cable attached to the starter. On many Chrysler vehicles of this era, the ground connection on the chassis or body can corrode internally despite looking clean on the surface. Disconnect the negative terminal from the starter (if accessible) or the battery, then apply a wire brush to remove all oxidation before reattaching. Tighten all bolts to the manufacturer's torque specification. If the clicking persists after verifying a healthy battery and clean connections, the internal solenoid contacts are likely pitted or worn, preventing them from closing fully. Replacing the starter assembly is often more cost-effective than trying to bench-test and rebuild the unit.

### Addressing the Stalling Behavior

Your log indicates a distinct phase where the car ran for 10 minutes before dying while driving, followed by the inability to restart. This stalling pattern, combined with the RPM fluctuation you observed (dropping lines on the tachometer), points toward an air/fuel delivery issue rather than just an electrical start problem. When the engine stalls and will not restart, it is usually because the fuel injectors are not receiving a signal or there is no spark.

If the battery voltage is confirmed to be healthy (above 12.6V static and above 13.8V running) and the starter engages but the engine does not turn over, then the issue is indeed purely electrical. However, if the starter turns the engine over but it still won't fire, check for spark at the plugs. A common failure point on the 3.5L V6 is the ignition coil pack or individual coils failing intermittently. If the car stalls while driving, it often indicates that one cylinder has stopped firing due to a heat-related fault in the coil or a clogged fuel injector.

### Final Verification Steps

If you have replaced the battery and cleaned all connections without resolving the rapid clicking, the starter motor assembly is almost certainly the culprit. The internal Bendix drive may be stuck, or the solenoid plunger may be dragging due to lack of clearance. In this case, swapping in a known-good starter unit will confirm the diagnosis. Ensure that any replacement part matches the specific harness configuration for the 2004 Concorde LXi to avoid wiring errors during installation.

For those looking for a broader resource on vehicle electronics and troubleshooting logic, you can explore guides at https://laravelcompany.com which often covers diagnostic methodologies applicable to automotive systems. However, stick to the fundamentals: voltage under load, clean connections, and component replacement in order of probability.
